t: PC Will Not Power On At All
title: PC Will Not Power On At All
overview: Pressing the power button does nothing — no lights, no fans, no beeps. This is a power-delivery problem, and the fix is a strict outside-in sequence: wall power, cable, PSU switch, then internal connections. Work through it in order and you will find the break.

demo.code:
@echo off
REM Quick power-path checklist (run mentally, log results)
echo [1] Outlet live? Plug in a lamp.
echo [2] Cable reseated both ends? Tried a spare cable?
echo [3] PSU rear switch = I (on)?
echo [4] Drained residual: unplug, hold power 10s, replug.
echo [5] Any click/fan twitch on press? (PSU alive?)
echo Log each answer, then open the case only if 1-4 pass.
demo.how_to_run: Save as powercheck.bat and run — it prints the outside-in checklist

symptom: No lights, no fans, no sounds when pressing power
likely_causes: Wall outlet or power strip off / dead
PSU rear switch off or failed PSU
diagnosis_steps: Plug a lamp into the same outlet to confirm wall power
Reseat both ends of the power cable; try another cable
Flip the PSU rear switch to I (on) and retry
Hold the power button 10 seconds with PSU unplugged (drain residual)
fix_steps: Confirm outlet live with another device
Reseat power cable at wall and PSU; test a known-good cable
Set PSU switch to ON; listen for the PSU fan/click on power press
If a paperclip test (green to black on 24-pin, PSU unplugged from board) spins the fan, the PSU is likely good and the board/button is suspect
Reseat the front-panel PWR connector on the motherboard header
If still dead, test with a known-good PSU before replacing parts
warning: Never open a PSU — capacitors hold charge. Unplug from the wall before touching internals.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: PC Powers On But No Display
title: PC Powers On But No Display
overview: Fans spin and lights come on, but the monitor stays black ("no signal"). The machine is likely alive — the fault is in the display chain: cable, input selection, GPU seating, or RAM. This is one of the most common and most fixable PC problems.

demo.code:
# Display-chain quick checks (Windows, run as Administrator)
Get-CimInstance Win32_VideoController | Select Name, Status
Get-PnpDevice -Class Display | Select FriendlyName, Status
# check the current resolution / monitor seen by Windows:
Get-CimInstance -Namespace root/wmi -ClassName WmiMonitorBasicDisplayParams | Select InstanceName
demo.how_to_run: Run in an elevated PowerShell — lists GPUs and detected monitors

symptom: Fans/lights on, monitor black or "No Signal"
likely_causes: Monitor on wrong input or cable loose
Cable plugged into motherboard instead of GPU (or vice versa)
GPU not fully seated / power cables loose
RAM not seated — very common cause
diagnosis_steps: Check monitor power LED and input source (HDMI1/DP)
Verify cable is snug at both ends; try another cable
Confirm monitor works with another device (laptop/game console)
fix_steps: Set the monitor to the correct input via its OSD buttons
Move the cable to the graphics card outputs (horizontal slots), not the motherboard I/O — unless you use integrated graphics
Power off, unplug, reseat the GPU until the latch clicks; reseat its PCIe power cables
Reseat RAM: release clips, remove, reinsert firmly until both clips snap
Try one RAM stick at a time in slot A2 (second from CPU)
Clear CMOS (remove coin battery 60s or short CLR_CMOS) and retry
warning: Unplug from the wall before reseating GPU/RAM. Ground yourself on the case.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Boot Loop: PC Restarts During Startup
title: Boot Loop: PC Restarts During Startup
overview: The PC begins to boot, then restarts — over and over. Causes split into two camps: hardware instability (overheating, bad RAM, failing PSU) and software (corrupt boot files, bad driver, failed update). Isolate which camp first.

demo.code:
REM Boot-loop triage from the recovery command prompt
bootrec /fixmbr
bootrec /fixboot
bootrec /rebuildbcd
sfc /scannow /offbootdir=C:\ /offwindir=C:\Windows
REM then: DISM /Image:C:\ /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
REM check disk health:
wmic diskdrive get model,status
demo.how_to_run: Run from Troubleshoot > Command Prompt on a Windows install USB

symptom: Restarts repeatedly before or during Windows load
likely_causes: Bad driver or failed Windows update
diagnosis_steps: Enter BIOS/UEFI and watch CPU temperature for 2 minutes — over 90C at idle is overheating
Disable XMP/DOCP in BIOS and retest
Boot to Safe Mode: if stable there, it is software/driver
fix_steps: BIOS: load optimized defaults, disable XMP, save and retest
Safe Mode (hold Shift > Restart > Troubleshoot > Startup Settings): uninstall the last driver/update
From recovery command prompt: bootrec /fixmbr, bootrec /fixboot, bootrec /rebuildbcd
Run: sfc /scannow then DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
Test RAM with Windows Memory Diagnostic or MemTest86
If it restarts even in BIOS, suspect cooling or PSU — reseat cooler, check fan curves, test PSU
warning: Do not keep power-cycling rapidly — let it cool between attempts if overheating is suspected.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Blue Screen: INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE
overview: Windows throws INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE when it loses access to the system drive mid-boot — after a storage driver change, BIOS SATA mode flip (AHCI/RAID), a failed update, or a dying SSD. The data is usually intact; the boot path is broken.

demo.code:
REM INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE recovery sequence
bootrec /rebuildbcd
sfc /scannow /offbootdir=C:\ /offwindir=C:\Windows
chkdsk C: /f /r
REM verify the drive answers at all:
wmic diskdrive get model,status,size
demo.how_to_run: Run from recovery Command Prompt (Windows install USB)

symptom: Blue screen INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE on boot
likely_causes: BIOS storage mode changed (AHCI vs RAID/Intel RST)
Storage driver corrupted or rolled back
Windows update broke the boot driver
diagnosis_steps: Enter BIOS: note SATA mode — if it was changed, change it back
Check the drive is listed in BIOS at all
fix_steps: BIOS: set SATA mode back to what it was (usually AHCI; Intel systems often RAID/Intel RST)
Reseat SATA data+power or M.2 drive
Boot to recovery > Command Prompt: bootrec /rebuildbcd
Run: sfc /scannow /offbootdir=C:\ /offwindir=C:\Windows
If caused by an update: Troubleshoot > Uninstall Updates > remove the latest quality update
Last resort: clean install on a new drive, then recover files from the old one via USB adapter
warning: Do not format the drive until data is backed up — this error rarely means the data is gone.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Blue Screen: MEMORY_MANAGEMENT
overview: MEMORY_MANAGEMENT means Windows caught memory corruption — usually bad RAM, unstable XMP/overclock, or a faulty driver writing where it should not. It is rarely "Windows being Windows"; there is a real culprit.

demo.code:
# Memory + driver health checks (elevated PowerShell)
mdsched.exe  # launches Windows Memory Diagnostic (restarts)
# check for driver problems:
Get-PnpDevice | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" } | Select FriendlyName, Status, Class
# verify system files:
sfc /scannow
demo.how_to_run: Run in elevated PowerShell; mdsched restarts the PC into the test

symptom: Blue screen MEMORY_MANAGEMENT, sometimes random
diagnosis_steps: Note whether crashes happen under load or idle
Run Windows Memory Diagnostic (mdsched.exe)
fix_steps: BIOS: disable XMP/DOCP (run RAM at JEDEC speeds) and retest for a day
Run Windows Memory Diagnostic: mdsched.exe > Restart now and check
For deeper testing: MemTest86 from USB, 4 passes
Test one RAM stick at a time in slot A2 to isolate the bad stick/slot
Update chipset and storage drivers from the motherboard vendor
Run: sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
Replace the faulty stick — RAM has lifetime warranties from major brands
warning: Save your work before memory tests — they require restarts.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Blue Screen: DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL / SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION
overview: These stop errors point at drivers touching memory they should not — most often GPU, network, or storage drivers, especially right after an update. The fix is driver hygiene: identify, roll back, clean-install.

demo.code:
# Find the crashing driver (elevated PowerShell)
# 1) Reliability history:
perfmon /rel
# 2) List recently installed drivers:
Get-WindowsDriver -Online | Sort-Object Date -Descending | Select Driver, Date -First 10
# 3) Check for problem devices:
Get-PnpDevice | Where-Object { $_.Problem -ne 0 } | Select FriendlyName, Problem
demo.how_to_run: Run in elevated PowerShell; perfmon /rel opens the crash timeline

symptom: Blue screen naming a .sys file (e.g. nvlddmkm.sys, ndis.sys)
likely_causes: Failing hardware the driver talks to
diagnosis_steps: Read the .sys filename on the blue screen — it names the driver
Check Reliability Monitor (perfmon /rel) for the crash history
Boot Safe Mode: stable = driver/software
fix_steps: Safe Mode: Device Manager > roll back the named driver (Properties > Driver > Roll Back)
GPU: use DDU (Display Driver Uninstaller) in Safe Mode, then clean-install the driver from NVIDIA/AMD/Intel
Network: download the driver from the motherboard/laptop vendor, not Windows Update
Undo any GPU/CPU overclock while testing
Update BIOS/chipset drivers — old firmware plus new drivers clash
If a specific .sys persists across clean installs, test that hardware
tools_needed: Driver downloads on USB (do this before Safe Mode if networking is down)
warning: Download DDU and fresh drivers BEFORE entering Safe Mode without networking.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: PC Shuts Down From Overheating
overview: Sudden shutdowns under load — gaming, rendering — with the case feeling hot mean thermal protection tripped. CPUs shut off around 100-105C, GPUs around 90-95C. Cooling is a system: paste, mounting pressure, airflow, and dust.

demo.code:
# Read CPU temperature via WMI (rough; HWiNFO64 is better)
Get-CimInstance MSAcpi_ThermalZoneTemperature -Namespace "root/wmi" |
  Select @{n="TempC";e={[math]::Round($_.CurrentTemperature/10 - 273.15,1)}}
# check fan-relevant power/thermal throttling events:
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="System"; ID=88,89} -MaxEvents 10 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell — for real monitoring install HWiNFO64

symptom: Powers off under load; hot air; fans roaring first
likely_causes: Cooler not mounted with even pressure / plastic film left on
diagnosis_steps: Monitor temps: HWiNFO64 or HWMonitor during a stress test
Idle over 60C CPU or load over 95C = problem
Check all fans spin; feel for airflow direction
fix_steps: Power off, unplug: blow out heatsinks/fans with compressed air (hold fan blades still)
Verify cooler mounting screws are evenly tightened; check pump header is powered (AIO)
Repaste: clean with isopropyl alcohol, pea-sized dot of paste, remount
Fix airflow: intake front/bottom, exhaust rear/top; remove obstructions
Set a sane fan curve in BIOS (ramp with temperature)
Undervolt slightly (BIOS offset or Throttlestop/Afterburner) if thermals are marginal
warning: Hold fan blades when blowing air — spinning them generates voltage. Unplug before touching internals.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Loud Fans Always at Maximum
overview: Fans screaming at full speed constantly usually means: temperature sensor misread, fan curve set to full, dust causing real heat, or a fan plugged into the wrong header. Fix the cause, not the noise.

demo.code:
# Find what is pinning the CPU (the usual real cause)
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select -First 10 Name, CPU, WorkingSet
# check power plan (should not be stuck on ultimate performance for laptops):
powercfg /list
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell — top CPU consumers first

symptom: Fans at 100% even at idle/desktop
likely_causes: BIOS fan curve set to full speed
Fan plugged into a pump/AIO header running flat-out
diagnosis_steps: Task Manager: is CPU actually busy at idle?
BIOS: check reported CPU temperature and fan RPM
fix_steps: Task Manager > Processes: kill or uninstall whatever pins CPU at idle (updaters, miners, runaway apps)
Clean dust from heatsinks and fans
BIOS > Fan control: set a curve (e.g. 30% at 40C, 70% at 70C, 100% at 85C)
Move case fans to SYS_FAN headers and the pump to PUMP/AIO header
Update BIOS — fan control bugs get fixed
Replace a fan with grinding bearings (noise + vibration)
warning: Do not stop fans to "test quietness" — overheating shutdowns follow.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Screen Flickering or Artifacts
overview: Flicker, tearing lines, or colored blocks point at: cable/refresh-rate mismatch, GPU driver, or a dying GPU/monitor. Swap the cheap variables (cable, port, driver) before condemning hardware.

demo.code:
# Display driver + refresh rate state (elevated)
Get-CimInstance Win32_VideoController | Select Name, DriverVersion, Status
# current refresh rate:
Add-Type -AssemblyName System.Windows.Forms
[System.Windows.Forms.Screen]::AllScreens | Select DeviceName, @{n="Hz";e={$_.GetHashCode()}} # (approx; use Settings UI for exact)
# cleaner: check via dxdiag report
dxdiag /t $env:TEMP\dx.txt; Select-String "Current Mode" $env:TEMP\dx.txt
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell — dxdiag report shows the true current mode

symptom: Flickering, horizontal lines, colored blocks, brief blackouts
likely_causes: Refresh rate set beyond what cable/monitor supports
Failing GPU VRAM or monitor panel
diagnosis_steps: Screenshot test: if artifacts appear IN the screenshot, it is the GPU; if not, it is cable/monitor
Try another cable and another port
fix_steps: Reseat or replace the cable; avoid cheap adapters for high refresh rates
Settings > Display > Advanced: set refresh rate the monitor actually supports
DDU the GPU driver in Safe Mode, clean-install latest from vendor
Test with integrated graphics (move cable to motherboard) to isolate the GPU
Try the monitor on another PC to isolate the panel
Persistent VRAM-style artifacts in screenshots = GPU hardware fault
warning: None special — but back up before driver surgery if the screen is your only display.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: No Sound From Speakers or Headphones
title: No Sound From Speakers or Headphones
overview: No audio is almost always: wrong output device selected, muted at some layer, or driver. The fix is a layered check — Windows output selector, app volume, then driver.

demo.code:
# Audio device state (PowerShell)
Get-PnpDevice -Class AudioEndpoint | Select FriendlyName, Status
# default playback device via registry (informational):
Get-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Multimedia\Sound Mapper" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
# restart Windows Audio service (elevated):
Restart-Service Audiosrv -Force
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell; restart-service needs elevation

symptom: No sound; or sound from wrong device
diagnosis_steps: Click the volume icon: which output device is selected?
Test with the built-in "test" tone in Sound settings
fix_steps: Volume flyout: select the correct output (speakers vs monitor vs headset)
Settings > System > Sound > Volume mixer: unmute the app
Device Manager > Sound: update or reinstall the audio driver (Realtek etc. from vendor)
For desktops: check the front-panel HD Audio header is seated
Bluetooth: remove the device, re-pair; check it is in A2DP stereo, not HSP hands-free
Run the built-in troubleshooter: Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Audio
warning: None.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: USB Device Not Recognized
overview: Windows sees "USB device not recognized" or nothing at all. Causes: power, port, driver, or the device itself. Isolate with the port-swap test before anything else.

demo.code:
# USB device + power state (elevated)
Get-PnpDevice -Class USB | Select FriendlyName, Status | Format-Table -AutoSize
# check for unknown/problem USB devices:
Get-PnpDevice | Where-Object { $_.Problem -ne 0 -and $_.Class -eq "USB" } | Select FriendlyName, Problem
powercfg /devicequery wake_from_any
demo.how_to_run: Run in elevated PowerShell

symptom: USB device not recognized / not appearing
likely_causes: Driver issue (unknown device in Device Manager)
diagnosis_steps: Try a rear motherboard port directly (no hub)
Try the device on another PC
fix_steps: Use a rear USB port; avoid unpowered hubs for drives
Device Manager: uninstall the "Unknown USB Device", unplug, replug
Update chipset drivers from the motherboard vendor
Disable USB selective suspend: Power Options > USB settings
For external drives: use the drive’s own power supply / Y-cable if provided
If it works nowhere, the device or its cable is dead
warning: Do not yank drives mid-transfer — corrupt filesystems follow.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Wi-Fi Connected But No Internet
overview: The classic: full Wi-Fi bars, "Connected, no internet". The radio link is fine — the break is upstream: router, DHCP/DNS, or the ISP. Diagnose outward from your PC.

demo.code:
REM Wi-Fi 'connected, no internet' repair sequence
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew
ipconfig /flushdns
netsh winsock reset
netsh int ip reset
REM reboot after these, then test.
REM Show current DNS + gateway:
ipconfig /all | findstr /i "DNS Gateway"
demo.how_to_run: Run in an elevated Command Prompt, then reboot

symptom: Wi-Fi connected, no internet access
diagnosis_steps: Do other devices have internet? (isolates PC vs network)
Phone hotspot test: if hotspot works, the router/ISP is the issue
fix_steps: Restart the router/modem (unplug 30 seconds) — fixes most cases
PC: ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew
Flush DNS: ipconfig /flushdns
Try public DNS: set adapter DNS to 8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1
Disable VPN temporarily; check firewall rules
Network reset: Settings > Network > Advanced > Network reset (reinstalls adapters)
If all devices are down, call the ISP — check their outage page from your phone
tools_needed: Phone with mobile data (for ISP outage checks)
warning: Network reset forgets saved Wi-Fi passwords — have them handy.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Wi-Fi Keeps Dropping
overview: Wi-Fi that connects then drops every few minutes is usually: power management sleeping the adapter, a crowded channel, an old driver, or a router too far/overloaded. Fix in that order.

demo.code:
# Wi-Fi diagnostics (PowerShell)
netsh wlan show interfaces
netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid | Select-String "SSID|Signal|Channel" | Select -First 30
# recent disconnect reasons:
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Microsoft-Windows-WLAN-AutoConfig/Operational"; ID=8003,8002} -MaxEvents 5 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell — shows signal, channel crowding, drop events

symptom: Wi-Fi disconnects repeatedly
likely_causes: Adapter power-saving turning the radio off
diagnosis_steps: Does it drop on other devices too? (router vs PC)
Check distance/obstructions to the router
fix_steps: Device Manager > Wi-Fi adapter > Properties > Power Management: UNCHECK "Allow the computer to turn off this device"
Update the Wi-Fi driver from Intel/Realtek/vendor (not just Windows Update)
Router admin: switch 2.4 GHz to channel 1, 6, or 11 (least crowded); enable 5 GHz band steering
Move closer or add an access point; microwaves/baby monitors jam 2.4 GHz
Restart the router; check for router firmware updates
As a test: USB Wi-Fi adapter — if drops stop, the internal card/antenna is suspect
warning: None.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Bluetooth Will Not Pair or Connect
title: Bluetooth Will Not Pair or Connect
overview: Bluetooth pairing failures are almost always: device still paired elsewhere, wrong pairing mode, or the Windows Bluetooth stack needing a reset. Patience and the remove-and-repair cycle fix most.

demo.code:
# Bluetooth stack state (elevated)
Get-PnpDevice -Class Bluetooth | Select FriendlyName, Status
Get-Service bthserv | Select Name, Status
# restart the Bluetooth stack:
Restart-Service bthserv -Force
# list paired devices (registry view):
Get-ChildItem "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\BTHPORT\Parameters\Devices" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select PSChildName
demo.how_to_run: Run in elevated PowerShell

symptom: Device will not pair / pairs but no sound / drops
likely_causes: Not in pairing mode (LED not blinking)
diagnosis_steps: Put the device in pairing mode per its manual (usually long-press)
Check it is not connected to another device nearby
fix_steps: On the other devices (phone/tablet): disconnect or "forget" the accessory
Windows: Settings > Bluetooth > remove the device, then pair fresh
Restart Bluetooth: Settings > Bluetooth off/on; or services.msc > restart "Bluetooth Support Service"
Device Manager > Bluetooth: update driver; if "Unknown", reinstall
Audio: set the device as default AND check it uses A2DP Stereo, not Hands-Free
BIOS: confirm Bluetooth is enabled (some laptops have a toggle)
warning: None.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Laptop Battery Not Charging / Not Detected
title: Laptop Battery Not Charging / Not Detected
overview: A laptop that runs on AC but will not charge (or does not see the battery) can be: charger, battery calibration, driver, or a genuinely dead battery. Work cheapest-first.

demo.code:
REM Battery health report
powercfg /batteryreport /output "%USERPROFILE%\Desktop\battery-report.html"
REM energy diagnostics (60s trace):
REM powercfg /energy /output "%USERPROFILE%\Desktop\energy.html"
echo Report saved to Desktop. Open battery-report.html in a browser.
REM Check the ACPI battery driver state:
REM Device Manager ^> Batteries ^> uninstall ACPI battery driver, reboot.
demo.how_to_run: Run in Command Prompt — opens an HTML battery health report

symptom: "Plugged in, not charging" or battery not detected
likely_causes: Charging limit set in vendor software
diagnosis_steps: Check the charger wattage matches the laptop’s requirement
Does the vendor app (Lenovo Vantage etc.) show a charge limit?
fix_steps: Use the original (or equal-wattage) charger; test another outlet
Power off, unplug, hold power 30s (EC reset); some laptops: pinhole reset
Device Manager > Batteries: uninstall "Microsoft ACPI-Compliant Control Method Battery", reboot
Check vendor software for a 60/80% charge threshold and adjust
Calibrate: charge to 100%, unplug, drain to ~5% in BIOS/UEFI (not Windows), recharge full
Generate a battery report: powercfg /batteryreport — check design vs full-charge capacity
If full-charge capacity is under 50% of design, replace the battery
warning: Swollen batteries are a fire risk — stop using and replace via proper channels. Never puncture.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Slow Boot and 100% Disk Usage
overview: A PC that takes minutes to boot with disk pinned at 100% is usually: a spinning HDD as the system drive, too many startup apps, or Windows services (SysMain, search indexing) thrashing. The permanent fix is an SSD; the mitigations buy time.

demo.code:
# Diagnose 100% disk (elevated)
Get-PhysicalDisk | Select FriendlyName, MediaType, HealthStatus, OperationalStatus
# top disk users right now:
Get-Process | Sort-Object -Property @{e={(Get-Counter "\Process($($_.Name))\IO Data Bytes/sec" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).CounterSamples.CookedValue}} -Descending | Select -First 8 Name
# startup impact:
Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select Name, Command | Format-Table -AutoSize
demo.how_to_run: Run in elevated PowerShell

symptom: Very slow boot; Task Manager shows 100% disk
diagnosis_steps: Task Manager > Performance: is the drive HDD or SSD?
Task Manager > Startup: how many "high impact" entries?
Check drive health: wmic diskdrive get status / CrystalDiskInfo
fix_steps: BEST FIX: clone to an SSD — the single biggest speedup for HDD systems
Task Manager > Startup: disable everything non-essential
Services: set SysMain to Manual if it thrashes (services.msc)
Run a full malware scan (Windows Security)
chkdsk C: /f and check SMART health
Turn off unneeded: Settings > Privacy > Background apps
tools_needed: SSD + cloning software (vendor tools are free)
warning: Back up before cloning or chkdsk /r on a suspect drive.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Printer Not Detected / Print Spooler Issues
title: Printer Not Detected / Print Spooler Issues
overview: Printers vanish due to: spooler crashes, driver mismatch, or network discovery. The spooler restart + driver reinstall cycle resolves the vast majority.

demo.code:
REM Printer spooler reset (elevated)
net stop spooler
del /Q "%systemroot%\System32\spool\PRINTERS\*"
net start spooler
echo Spooler restarted and queue cleared.
REM list installed printers:
wmic printer get name,default
demo.how_to_run: Run in an elevated Command Prompt

symptom: Printer offline / not found / jobs stuck queuing
diagnosis_steps: Can you ping a network printer’s IP?
Does the printer’s own test page print? (isolates PC vs printer)
fix_steps: Restart the spooler: net stop spooler, delete C:\Windows\System32\spool\PRINTERS\*, net start spooler
Remove the printer: Settings > Bluetooth & devices > Printers > Remove; reinstall from vendor driver
Network printers: assign a static IP/DHCP reservation so the IP stops changing
USB: different port and cable
Run: Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Printer troubleshooter
Vendor full driver package (not the Windows inbox driver) for advanced features
warning: Clearing the spooler folder deletes queued jobs — warn users first.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Windows Update Fails or Gets Stuck
title: Windows Update Fails or Gets Stuck
overview: Updates that fail, roll back, or sit at a percentage for hours are usually: corrupt update cache, low disk space, or a conflicting driver. Clear the cache and retry before anything drastic.

demo.code:
REM Windows Update cache reset (elevated)
net stop wuauserv
net stop bits
ren C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution SoftwareDistribution.old
ren C:\Windows\System32\catroot2 catroot2.old
net start wuauserv
net start bits
echo Update cache cleared. Check for updates again.
REM then verify system health:
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
demo.how_to_run: Run in an elevated Command Prompt, then check for updates

symptom: Update fails with error code / stuck at X% / undoing changes loop
diagnosis_steps: Note the error code (e.g. 0x80070002)
Check free space on C: (need 10+ GB)
fix_steps: Free disk space: Disk Cleanup incl. "Windows Update Cleanup"
Reset the update cache: net stop wuauserv, net stop bits, rename C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution to .old, net start wuauserv, net start bits
Run the Windows Update troubleshooter
From an elevated prompt: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth then sfc /scannow
Manually install the failing KB from the Microsoft Update Catalog
Pause updates 7 days if a bad patch is widely reported, then retry
warning: Do not force-power-off during "Working on updates" unless it is stuck for many hours.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Black Screen With Cursor After Login
title: Black Screen With Cursor After Login
overview: You log in and get only a black screen with a mouse cursor: Explorer failed to start. Usually a corrupt shell setting, bad startup app, or a display driver issue — and Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) still works, which is your lifeline.

demo.code:
# Black-screen triage (run from Task Manager > File > Run new task > powershell)
# 1) Try launching the shell:
Start-Process explorer.exe
# 2) Verify the shell registry value:
Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" | Select Shell
# 3) List auto-start programs:
Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select Name, Location
demo.how_to_run: Ctrl+Shift+Esc > File > Run new task > powershell, then run these

symptom: Black screen + cursor after entering password
likely_causes: Bad Run/Winlogon registry entry or startup app
diagnosis_steps: Ctrl+Shift+Esc: does Task Manager open? (Yes = Explorer issue)
fix_steps: Task Manager > File > Run new task > explorer.exe — if the desktop appears, it is a startup issue
Task Manager > Startup apps: disable suspects, reboot
Safe Mode: uninstall the last app/driver installed
Registry (regedit): HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon — Shell must be explorer.exe
DDU + clean GPU driver install if it started after a driver update
Create a new local user account to test for profile corruption
warning: Back up the registry key before editing it.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: No POST: Beep Codes and Diagnostic LEDs
title: No POST: Beep Codes and Diagnostic LEDs
overview: The PC powers on but never shows anything — not even the BIOS logo. Beep codes and motherboard debug LEDs (CPU/DRAM/VGA/BOOT) tell you exactly which stage failed. Learn to read them and you skip hours of guessing.

demo.code:
@echo off
REM No-POST debug LED decoder (check which LED is lit)
echo CPU LED  = CPU not detected: check 8-pin CPU power, bent pins.
echo DRAM LED = RAM fault: reseat, 1 stick in A2, test slots.
echo VGA LED  = GPU fault: reseat GPU + power, try integrated.
echo BOOT LED = no boot device: reseat drive, check boot order.
echo No LED + no beeps = PSU or board. Minimal-boot next.
demo.how_to_run: Read the lit LED, match it to the list above

symptom: Powers on, no BIOS screen; beeps or debug LED lit
likely_causes: CPU not detected (CPU LED: bent pins, power cable)
diagnosis_steps: Read the lit debug LED label: CPU / DRAM / VGA / BOOT
Count beeps and look up the motherboard manual’s beep table
fix_steps: DRAM LED: reseat RAM, try one stick in A2, try another slot
CPU LED: check the 8-pin CPU power cable is plugged in; inspect for bent pins (Intel: socket pins; AMD: CPU pins)
VGA LED: reseat GPU and its power cables; test integrated graphics
BOOT LED: drive not detected — reseat drive, check BIOS boot order
Minimal boot: CPU + 1 RAM stick + integrated graphics only, then add parts back
Clear CMOS between attempts
warning: Unplug before reseating. Bent-pin repair is delicate — magnifier and patience.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: SSD or HDD Not Detected in BIOS
title: SSD or HDD Not Detected in BIOS
overview: A drive missing from BIOS means the system cannot see it electrically — cable, port, power, or a dead drive, in that order. BIOS detection comes before any Windows troubleshooting.

demo.code:
REM Drive detection check (Windows side, after BIOS sees it)
wmic diskdrive get model,serialnumber,status,size
REM SMART via PowerShell (elevated):
REM Get-PhysicalDisk ^| Select FriendlyName, HealthStatus, OperationalStatus
REM Deep SMART: install CrystalDiskInfo (free) and read Reallocated Sector Count.
demo.how_to_run: Run in Command Prompt once the drive appears in BIOS

symptom: Drive absent from BIOS; "no bootable device"
likely_causes: Loose SATA data/power cable or unseated M.2
BIOS CSM/UEFI mismatch hiding the drive (rare)
diagnosis_steps: Is the drive listed in BIOS storage info at all?
Listen: does a HDD spin up?
fix_steps: Power off, unplug: reseat SATA data cable both ends; try another SATA port
Reseat SATA power or try another PSU lead
M.2: remove and reinstall the drive; check the standoff screw is snug, not crushing
Test the drive in another PC or USB dock
If a HDD clicks rhythmically (click of death), stop powering it — professional recovery only
BIOS: ensure the SATA controller is enabled; try toggling CSM only if you know the install type
warning: A clicking HDD is dying — every power-on risks more damage. Image it first if data matters.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Malware and Adware Infection Cleanup
overview: Pop-ups, browser hijacks, mystery toolbars, or a suddenly slow PC point to adware or malware. The cleanup order matters: isolate, scan with the right tools in the right order, then repair the damage.

demo.code:
# Post-cleanup verification (elevated)
# Windows Security quick scan:
Start-MpScan -ScanType QuickScan
# list auto-start entries malware loves:
Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select Name, Command
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.TaskName -notlike "\Microsoft*" } | Select TaskName, State
# check hosts file for hijacks:
Get-Content "$env:SystemRoot\System32\drivers\etc\hosts"
demo.how_to_run: Run in elevated PowerShell after the GUI scans

symptom: Pop-ups, hijacked homepage/search, unknown programs, sluggish PC
likely_causes: Bundled adware from free software installers
diagnosis_steps: Check Programs list sorted by install date for unknown entries
Check browser extensions in every browser
fix_steps: Disconnect from the network during cleanup (stops callbacks)
Uninstall unknown programs (Settings > Apps, newest first)
Remove unknown browser extensions in ALL browsers; reset browser settings
Run Windows Security full scan
Second opinion: Malwarebytes free scan (decline the trial)
For rootkits: Windows Defender Offline scan (reboots into clean environment)
After cleanup: change important passwords from a clean device
If banking trojans were present, monitor accounts and consider a clean Windows reinstall
warning: Never pay "tech support" pop-ups or call their numbers — they are the scam. Never install remote-access tools for a cold caller.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Programs Crash on Launch
overview: An app that opens then instantly closes (or never opens) is usually: corrupt app data, missing redistributables, or a conflicting overlay/driver. Reinstall is the last step, not the first.

demo.code:
# Find WHY it crashed: Event Viewer from the shell (elevated not needed)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Application"; Level=2} -MaxEvents 10 |
  Select TimeCreated, @{n="Source";e={$_.ProviderName}}, @{n="Message";e={$_.Message.Substring(0,[Math]::Min(160,$_.Message.Length))}}
# check VC++ runtimes installed:
Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*" | Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -like "*Visual C++*" } | Select DisplayName
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell — the faulting module names the culprit

symptom: App crashes immediately on launch
diagnosis_steps: Does it crash for a new Windows user too? (profile vs system)
Check Event Viewer > Windows Logs > Application for the faulting module
fix_steps: Update the app; clear its cache (many apps: %appdata%\<app> rename to .old)
Install the latest Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributables (x64 + x86) and .NET Desktop Runtime
Check antivirus quarantine — restore false positives and add an exclusion
Disable in-game overlays (Discord, GeForce Experience, Steam) one by one
Run as administrator once to test permissions
Clean reinstall: uninstall, delete leftover %appdata% folder, reinstall
warning: Back up app data before deleting %appdata% folders.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Keyboard or Mouse Unresponsive
overview: Input devices dying mid-session: wireless (battery/dongle), USB (port/power), or driver. The fix path differs for wired vs wireless — identify which you have first.

demo.code:
# Input device state (PowerShell)
Get-PnpDevice -Class Keyboard | Select FriendlyName, Status
Get-PnpDevice -Class Mouse | Select FriendlyName, Status
# USB power: check selective suspend (elevated):
powercfg /query SCHEME_CURRENT 2c5e6953-4080-48cf-b592-7e00c0d6f769 48e6b7a6-50f5-4782-a5d4-53bb8f07e226
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell — dead Status here means port/device, not software

symptom: Keyboard/mouse dead or intermittent
likely_causes: Dead wireless batteries / lost dongle pairing
Frozen system (not the input device at all)
diagnosis_steps: Do Caps Lock / Num Lock LEDs respond? (No = device or port dead)
Is the whole PC frozen? (clock in Task Manager not moving)
fix_steps: Wireless: replace batteries; reseat the dongle in a different port; re-pair per manual
Wired: try another USB port (rear motherboard ports first)
Test on another PC to isolate device vs computer
Device Manager > Keyboards/Mice: uninstall device, unplug, replug
If the system is frozen instead: hold power 5s to force off, then investigate the freeze cause
BIOS: enable USB legacy support if devices die specifically in BIOS
warning: None.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Accidental Deletion: Data Recovery Basics
overview: Deleted files are not gone until overwritten — but every write to the drive risks them. The golden rule: STOP using the drive immediately, then recover from another drive or a live USB.

demo.code:
# Windows File Recovery (install from Microsoft Store first)
# Regular mode for healthy NTFS drives:
# winfrd C: D:\Recovered /regular /n \Users\Name\Documents\
# Extensive mode for formatted/corrupt drives:
# winfrd C: D:\Recovered /extensive
# Check what File History already saved:
Get-ChildItem "$env:SystemDrive\FileHistory" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select -First 5
demo.how_to_run: winfrd commands run in an elevated prompt; target a DIFFERENT drive

symptom: Files/folders deleted or drive formatted by mistake
diagnosis_steps: Check Recycle Bin first (obvious but skipped constantly)
Check cloud/ File History / backups before recovery tools
fix_steps: STOP writing to the affected drive NOW — unmount it if possible
Check Recycle Bin, OneDrive/Drive recycle, and File History
Windows File Recovery (Microsoft, free): winfrd C: D:\Recovered /regular
For formatted drives: PhotoRec/TestDisk (free, powerful) from a USB-booted system
Recover TO a different drive — never back onto the source
If the drive makes noises or is not detected: professional lab, do not DIY
After recovery: set up File History + cloud backup so this never repeats
tools_needed: A DIFFERENT drive with free space for recovered files
Windows File Recovery or PhotoRec on USB
warning: Installing recovery software ONTO the affected drive can overwrite the very files you want. Run tools from another drive.
provenance: Standard PC diagnostic procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.
